# Converting a wealth gradient to OG-Core's units

The library's wealth gradient is the slope of the log rate on household wealth
rank (0 to 1). OG-Core (version 0.18 and later) parameterizes differences
across lifetime-income groups as a slope in the **log-odds** of the rate per
**centered percentile point**, and generates group-specific rates with a
mean-preserving logistic function that keeps the UN rate at each age and
period. Two conversions follow.

1. **Rank to percentile points.** OG-Core places each income group at its
   centered percentile midpoint (−40, −20, 0, +20, +40 for quintiles), so the
   gradient is divided by 100.
2. **Log rate to log odds.** The gradient is divided by (1 − p), where p is
   OG-Core's own rate at that age and period on its own scale: births per
   person per year for fertility (OG-Core divides the UN rate per 1,000 women by
   2,000) and the annual probability of death for mortality.

The value passed to OG-Core is therefore

    gradient / (100 × (1 − p))

Because p varies by age, a converted fertility gradient is a vector by age.
The rates p should be those OG-Core itself uses (the UN schedule downloaded in
the calibration), not the survey rates.

## Size of the correction

Every complete DHS quintile set for infant mortality, under-five mortality and
age-specific fertility was passed through `_mean_preserving_logit_rates` from
OG-Core v0.24.1, at OG-Core's own scaling
([`scripts/check_ogcore_units.py`](../../scripts/check_ogcore_units.py); results in
[`data/ogcore_units_check.csv`](../../data/ogcore_units_check.csv)). The table
reports the change in the low/high ratio that OG-Core produces when given
`gradient / 100` instead of the converted value; a negative number means the
differential is understated.

| Rate | Quintile sets | Median rate p | Change, median (%) | Change, 10th percentile (%) | Remaining after conversion (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mortality, ages 0–4 | 291 | 0.016 | −0.97 | −2.40 | −0.17 |
| Infant mortality | 292 | 0.053 | −2.61 | −5.52 | −0.21 |
| Fertility, ages 15–19 | 313 | 0.050 | −5.44 | −8.89 | −0.44 |
| Fertility, ages 20–24 | 313 | 0.105 | −6.66 | −10.32 | −0.32 |
| Fertility, ages 25–29 | 313 | 0.106 | −4.51 | −7.75 | −0.10 |
| Fertility, ages 30–34 | 312 | 0.092 | −3.83 | −7.34 | −0.09 |
| Fertility, ages 35–39 | 310 | 0.064 | −3.41 | −6.82 | −0.25 |
| Fertility, ages 40–44 | 294 | 0.030 | −2.66 | −5.63 | −0.76 |
| Fertility, ages 45–49 | 129 | 0.011 | −1.32 | −3.99 | −3.07 |

Without the (1 − p) term, the slope passed to OG-Core is too small by the
factor (1 − p): at the median rates in the table, by 1–11
percent for fertility and 5
percent for infant mortality. As a result, the low/high ratio that OG-Core
produces is too small by 1.32–6.66 percent for fertility and
2.61 percent for infant mortality
(table). Adult death rates are low (median annual rate 0.012, maximum
0.061 in the library), so for adult mortality the slope is too small by
about 1 percent at the median rate and at most 6 percent. Adult
mortality quintile sets were not included in the test.

The last column compares the converted value with the slope that best
reproduces the measured quintile rates through OG-Core's function. It is
within 1 percent for every rate except fertility, ages 45-49, where rates are lowest and quintile estimates least precise. Remaining differences reflect
non-monotonic quintile rates that no single slope can fit.

## Other conventions

Signs agree: a negative value means higher rates in poorer groups in both the
library and OG-Core. The library provides no grouping: OG-Core derives each
group's midpoint from the `lambdas` passed to it, so the same converted value
applies to any number and size of income groups.
